summary: Gives guidelines for optional services that Internet Fax Gateways may offer, complementing the base requirements. These gateways link the telephone fax network with email-based Internet fax. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If a bridge between fax and email is the basic service, this memo lists the extra things it might offer, like bonus lanes on a road.

subtitle: Optional features for gateways connecting email and telephone faxes.

tldr.problem: Internet Fax Gateways bridge telephone fax networks and email-based internet fax, but their optional features—such as duplicate detection, automatic retries, and error handling—are not standardized.
tldr.mechanism: This document recommends optional services that gateways should implement, including techniques to drop duplicate messages, handle recoverable and non-recoverable errors, manage retransmissions, and maintain activity logs.
tldr.outcome: The recommendations help gateways work more reliably and consistently, reducing message loss and user confusion when fax networks and internet mail interact.

facts.label: Gateway types
facts.value: Offramp (internet to phone) and onramp (phone to internet)

facts.label: Authorization methods for onramp
facts.value: Caller-ID, station ID, or DTMF tones

today: RFC 4161 is an Informational RFC providing guidelines, not a standard. The recommendations in it remain relevant for operators setting up internet fax gateways, though adoption of these optional services varies by vendor.

sections.title: What Internet Fax Gateways Do
sections.content:
An Internet Fax Gateway bridges traditional switched telephone network (GSTN) faxes with email-based internet faxes, letting telephone fax machines and email users exchange documents. The gateway works in two directions: an offramp gateway converts internet faxes into telephone fax transmissions, while an onramp gateway does the opposite, converting telephone faxes into email messages.

The RFC describes optional services that gateways may offer beyond basic connectivity. These services include techniques for removing duplicate messages, automatically retrying failed transmissions, distinguishing between recoverable and non-recoverable errors, and maintaining detailed logs of gateway activity. The recommendations apply only to store-and-forward operation, where messages are held temporarily, not to real-time fax services.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway is like a postal worker who takes a fax from a phone machine and turns it into an email, or the opposite. This memo lists extra things that postal worker could do, like making sure two copies don't arrive and keeping a notebook of all the mail.

sections.title: Offramp Gateway Services
sections.content:
When an internet fax travels through an offramp gateway toward the telephone network, problems can arise. Multiple recipients in a single email message might result in the gateway receiving duplicate copies, especially if the mail transport system delivers one copy per recipient. To prevent sending the same fax multiple times to the same telephone number, the gateway SHOULD use the SMTP envelope address from the RCPT TO field if available, or check the message's Message-ID header to detect and skip already-processed messages.

When transmission fails, the gateway must decide whether to retry. Recoverable errors like busy signals or missing carrier signals should trigger automatic retransmission attempts later. Non-recoverable errors like paper jams or voice responses should not. For recoverable errors, administrators should be able to configure retry counts and intervals. The gateway SHOULD avoid retransmitting pages that already arrived successfully.

When sending delivery notifications back to the email sender, the gateway faces a choice: send a notice immediately after each recipient's outcome, or gather results and send one notice for many recipients. If the gateway fails to send a notice, it SHOULD try again later; if that also fails, it should log the error and alert administrators.
sections.plainLanguage: When a gateway sends a fax through the phone network, it might get a busy signal, which means try again later. If it gets a message saying the paper jammed, there is no point trying. The gateway should keep notes and send back a message to say whether it worked.

sections.title: Onramp Gateway Services
sections.content:
When a onramp gateway receives a fax from the telephone network, it should verify that the caller is authorized to transmit into the internet fax service. The RFC suggests several authorization methods. The simplest is to check the caller's GSTN caller-ID, which the telephone network generates and is difficult to forge. The gateway administrator maintains a table of permitted caller IDs, matched directly or with wildcards.

Alternatively, the gateway can extract the fax terminal's station ID—an alphanumeric string sent during the initial fax negotiation—and use it to look up user credentials embedded in that string. This method is more flexible because it does not tie authorization to a single physical device, but it is less secure because the user controls the string and it travels in plain text.

A third method asks the caller to send a user ID and password as DTMF (Dual Tone Multi-Frequency) tones after the call connects but before fax transmission begins. The RFC warns that sending passwords in plain form is a high security risk. Like offramp gateways, onramp gateways SHOULD maintain logs recording the start and end times of transmission, pages received, fax resolution, error codes, sender address, delivery attempts, and final outcome.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway that receives a fax from a phone should check that the person sending it is allowed to. It can check the phone number it came from, ask for a password sent as beeps, or extract secret code from the fax machine's name. The gateway should keep a log of everything it does.

sections.title: Security Concerns
sections.content:
The main security question is how the onramp gateway authorizes telephone senders. Caller-ID authorization is secure if the telephone network's caller-ID service is trustworthy. Station ID authorization, by itself, is weak because the user can choose what string to send and it travels unencrypted. Combining caller-ID with station ID checks provides better security than either alone.

Internet Fax messages can be signed or encrypted with S/MIME or OpenPGP, but when a message reaches a gateway, either onramp or offramp, those protections break down. The gateway must open the message to forward it, so the end-to-end security provided by these technologies ends at the gateway. Gateway administrators SHOULD use strong authentication and access controls for the gateway itself. Other security mechanisms like IPsec or TLS do not solve the fundamental problem of the gateway being a trust boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone caller-ID is hard to fake, so checking it is safe. Passwords sent as phone beeps are not safe because anyone listening could hear them. The gateway is a risky place for secret information because it has to open the message to send it on, so it cannot use end-to-end encryption.
